title: Tuwo Masara
localName: Tuwo masara — tuo masara, corn tuwo
author: Ronke Adeyemi
desc: Two cups of corn flour to three of water, stirred continuously until thick and stretchy, then a quarter cup more water and three minutes covered on the lowest heat.
longDesc: Of the three tuwos this is the only one with a usable ratio, and it is a genuinely quick swallow: corn flour and water go into the pot cold together and are stirred over medium heat until the mixture is thick and stretchy. Then a quarter cup of extra water goes in, the heat drops to minimum, and the pot sits covered for three minutes before a final stir to smooth. Fifteen minutes from start to finish. Note that the extra quarter cup is in the method but not the ingredient list, so the real total is three and a quarter cups.
ingredients: 1/4 cup water, added later — see the note
steps: Combine the corn flour and the 3 cups of water in a medium pot.
Place on medium heat and stir continuously until the mixture is thick and stretchy.
Reduce the heat to minimum and leave the pot covered for 3 minutes.
chefTips: Two cups of flour to three of water, plus the extra quarter cup. That is the only usable tuwo ratio in any source consulted.
Thick and stretchy is the cue before the extra water goes in. Stretchy is the operative word — it should pull away from the spoon.
Cold start, both together. Corn flour into hot water will lump immediately.
Stir continuously, not occasionally. The whole first stage is constant movement.
The covered three minutes on minimum heat is a steaming stage. Do not lift the lid.
The extra quarter cup is in the method but not the ingredient list, so the list's three cups understates the total. That discrepancy is in the source.

Tuwo masara starts from a dry flour stirred into water. Tuwo shinkafa starts from whole grains cooked and then mashed (NGA086) — a genuinely different technique, and the only thing distinguishing the tuwos is the grain and that.
commonMistakes: Adding the flour to water that is already hot.
Lifting the lid during the three minutes.
Using only the three cups listed and wondering why it is stiff.
sources: Adapted from 'Tuwo (Tuo) Masara (Corn Tuwo)', byline Ronke Edoho, 9jafoodie. Quantities exactly as printed: 2 cups corn flour; 3 cups water.

The method is verbatim and complete: 'Combine the Corn flour and water in a medium pot, place on medium heat and stir continuously until the mixture is thick and stretchy. Add ¼ cup of water, reduce the heat to minimum and leave the pot covered for 3mins. Stir until smooth.' Yield not specified.

INGREDIENT/METHOD DISCREPANCY, flagged: the method calls for '¼ cup of water' IN ADDITION to the 3 cups in the ingredient list, which the list does not account for. Total water is therefore 3 1/4 cups, not 3. Both figures are carried above with a note.

THIS IS THE ONLY TUWO OF THE THREE WITH A USABLE FLOUR-TO-WATER RATIO. All Nigerian Recipes' tuwo shinkafa — the most-cited source for that dish — contains NO QUANTITIES AT ALL (NGA086). Tuwo dawa, the guinea corn or sorghum version, returned NOTHING from any named source: targeted searches across All Nigerian Recipes, Nigerian Food TV, 9jafoodie, Kitchen Butterfly, Dobby's Signature, Sisi Jemimah and Daily Trust surfaced no citable recipe. That gap is recorded rather than filled, and tuwo dawa is not published in this collection.

WHAT ACTUALLY DISTINGUISHES THE TUWOS, on the evidence: the grain, and the technique that follows from it. Tuwo masara starts from a dry flour stirred into water as a paste; tuwo shinkafa starts from whole soft rice grains cooked and then mashed. That is a real difference — flour-then-stir against grain-then-mash. But NO source consulted sets the three side by side and says so, and tuwo dawa is absent entirely, so whether dawa follows the flour method or the grain method is not documented. It is not assumed here.

The same site's headnote pairs this with 'Miyan wake (Gbegiri) and sauced oxtail', which is a useful cross-regional identification — miyan wake is the northern name for the bean soup the Yoruba call gbegiri (NGA004).
storage: Eat the same day. It firms within the hour.
reheating: Steam, or microwave wrapped in damp cling film.
healthBenefits: Fat-free as cooked — nothing goes in but flour and water.
Corn supplies fibre and B vitamins.
culturalNote: Tuwo is the northern swallow and the grain names the dish: masara for corn, shinkafa for rice, dawa for guinea corn. It goes under the miyan soups — kuka, taushe, zogale — and the pairing is as fixed in the north as amala with gbegiri is in Ibadan. That the corn version is the one with a written ratio is probably because flour is easier to measure than a pot of softened rice.
